children: Foghorn Therapeutics said it would be slashing nearly half of its workforce after scrapping a drug development partnership with Eli Lilly, forcing the biotech into defensive mode as it attempts to conserve cash.

The Massachusetts-based biotech, valued at roughly $212 million, announced Thursday that it and Lilly had decided not to advance a cancer drug candidate, FHD-909, into the next phase of clinical testing following an early-stage dose escalation trial.
Foghorn added that the companies also were scrapping a second collaborative cancer program and don't anticipate any further joint projects.
Foghorn stock sank 16% to $3, putting it on track for its worst single-day drop since November 2025, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Lilly, meanwhile, ticked slightly lower.

The efficacy of the drugmaker's former lead asset, FHD-909, depended on a biological concept called synthetic lethality, where a cancer cell can survive losing one protein but dies if it loses a second backup protein.

Though promising in early testing, synthetic lethality "has not translated into the level of efficacy required to further advance the program," Foghorn CEO Adrian Gottschalk said. Following the setback, Gottschalk noted that Foghorn will redirect its resources to advance other pipeline programs.

The biotech plans to reduce its head count by roughly 40% and cut costs to extend its cash runway. Foghorn expects to be able to fund its most important research projects into the second half of 2029, including a novel immunology program and two cancer programs for drugs targeting specific proteins.
Citizens analyst Silvan Turkcan moved to the sidelines following the dissolution of the partnership. He now rates Foghorn stock at Market Perform, down from Market Outperform, with no price target.

In Turkcan's view, Foghorn lacks "near-term catalysts around remaining assets," as shares trade at a slight premium to the company's cash reserves. "We view shares as fairly valued, consistent with biotech peers facing similar uncertainties as Foghorn prioritizes its pre-clinical programs," he wrote.

Lilly, through its Loxo Oncology division, partnered with Foghorn Therapeutics in December 2021 to create novel oncology medicines. The deal included $300 million in upfront cash for the collaboration, plus an $80 million equity investment from Lilly at $20 a share.
